definition: The dappled, shifting sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees.
exampleSentence: We lay on the moss and watched the komorebi tremble gold across our hands.
etymology: Japanese 木漏れ日, from 木 'ko' (tree) + 漏れ 'more' (leaking through) + 日 'bi' (sunlight); literally 'sunlight that leaks through trees'.

definition: The shimmering trail of moonlight or other light reflected on water at night.
exampleSentence: From the ferry we watched the yakamoz stretch like spilled silver toward the city.
etymology: Turkish, ultimately from Greek; once also the phosphorescence of sea plankton, now chiefly the glitter of moonlight on water.

definition: The trance-like ecstasy or rapture that music can induce in listener and performer alike.
exampleSentence: By the third song the whole café had surrendered to tarab, swaying with closed eyes.
etymology: Arabic طرب, from the root ṭ-r-b 'to be moved or delighted'; the merging of musical and emotional enchantment.

definition: An unhurried coffee-and-pastry break taken with others purely for the pleasure of pausing together.
exampleSentence: The whole office stops at three for fika, and no one dares schedule a meeting over it.
etymology: Swedish, a playful back-slang reversal of the old word 'kaffi' (coffee); the social ritual around the cup, not just the drink.

definition: The act of tenderly running your fingers through the hair of someone you love.
exampleSentence: She fell asleep mid-sentence as he gave her slow cafuné on the sofa.
etymology: Brazilian Portuguese, of African (likely Bantu) origin carried into Brazil; an everyday gesture of tenderness with no English equivalent.

definition: The excess weight gained from comfort-eating one's way through grief or stress.
exampleSentence: Three months of breakup ice cream left him with a soft layer of kummerspeck.
etymology: German, from 'Kummer' (grief) + 'Speck' (bacon, fat); literally 'grief bacon'. Recorded in the Collins German–English Dictionary.

definition: The perfect, witty comeback that arrives only after the moment to use it has passed.
exampleSentence: Halfway down the stairs the devastating treppenwitz finally came to her, far too late.
etymology: German, from 'Treppe' (stairs) + 'Witz' (joke); a 'staircase joke', calquing the French 'esprit de l'escalier'. In the Collins German–English Dictionary.

definition: An aching homesickness for far-off places you have never even been to.
exampleSentence: A single train timetable was enough to flood him with restless fernweh.
etymology: German, from 'fern' (far) + 'Weh' (woe, ache); literally 'far-sickness', the mirror image of Heimweh (homesickness).

definition: The seemingly malicious behaviour of inanimate objects that conspire to thwart us.
exampleSentence: The printer jamming five minutes before the deadline was pure resistentialism.
etymology: Coined in 1948 by humorist Paul Jennings in 'Report on Resistentialism' (The Spectator); a blend of Latin 'res' (thing) + French 'résister' + 'existentialism', spoofing Sartre. Slogan: 'Les choses sont contre nous'.

definition: A face so smug or irritating that it seems to be begging for a slap.
exampleSentence: The contestant's gloating smirk was a textbook backpfeifengesicht.
etymology: German, from 'Backpfeife' (a slap on the cheek) + 'Gesicht' (face); literally 'a face that needs slapping'.

definition: A peace-offering gift brought home to mollify a partner you have annoyed.
exampleSentence: He arrived an hour late clutching tulips and chocolate — unmistakable drachenfutter.
etymology: German, from 'Drache' (dragon) + 'Futter' (fodder); literally 'dragon-fodder', the appeasing offering laid before the beast.

definition: The involuntary cinema of the mind that plays out vivid imagined scenes.
exampleSentence: One unread text and her kopfkino was already screening three disaster sequels.
etymology: German, from 'Kopf' (head) + 'Kino' (cinema); literally 'head cinema'.

definition: The dispiriting state of looking worse after a haircut than you did before it.
exampleSentence: He left the barber's in full age-otori, hat jammed low over his ears.
etymology: Japanese 上げ劣り, from 'age' (to cut/raise) + 'otori' (inferior); coming out looking inferior to before.

definition: The day after tomorrow, expressed in a single tidy word.
exampleSentence: Not tomorrow, not today — let's settle it on zeg, when the rush is over.
etymology: Georgian ზეგ; part of a full series of day-words including 'mazeg', two days hence. Recorded in Chubinashvili's nineteenth-century Georgian dictionary.

definition: A joke so clumsily told and unfunny that you cannot help laughing anyway.
exampleSentence: His pun was such a jayus that the whole table groaned and then cracked up.
etymology: Indonesian slang; a joke whose comedic value comes precisely from its spectacular failure to be funny.

definition: Weather that looks beautiful through the window but is miserable to be out in.
exampleSentence: Bright sun, bitter wind — classic gluggaveður, so we stayed in with cocoa.
etymology: Icelandic, from 'gluggi' (window) + 'veður' (weather); literally 'window-weather'.

definition: Food packed for a journey but carried back home uneaten, now somehow a small treat.
exampleSentence: The kids begged for the squashed madárlátta sandwiches the moment we got home.
etymology: Hungarian, from the phrase 'a madár látta' — 'the bird saw it'; leftover picnic food the birds glimpsed but no one ate. In Hungarian academic dictionaries.

definition: A person who turns up to mourn at a wake mainly for the free refreshments.
exampleSentence: Every funeral in town drew the same pesamenteiro, weeping near the buffet.
etymology: Portuguese, from 'pêsames' (condolences) + the agentive suffix '-eiro'; one who 'does condolences', chiefly for the food.

definition: The damp ring a cold, sweating glass leaves behind on a table.
exampleSentence: Three culaccini overlapped on the wood where our drinks had stood all afternoon.
etymology: Italian, a diminutive based on 'culaccio'; the little mark left by the bottom of a wet glass.

definition: The rush of joy felt on reuniting with someone after a long time apart.
exampleSentence: The airport arrivals hall was a sea of tearful retrouvailles and crushed bouquets.
etymology: French, from 'retrouver' (to find again); literally 'rediscoveries', the happiness of meeting again.

definition: The quiet certainty, on first meeting someone, that the two of you will fall in love.
exampleSentence: It wasn't love at first sight, just koi no yokan — a sense of what was coming.
etymology: Japanese 恋の予感, from 'koi' (love) + 'no' (of) + 'yokan' (premonition); the premonition of love rather than love itself.

definition: The giddy disorientation of being far from home in an unfamiliar country.
exampleSentence: The unfamiliar smells and signage filled her with a thrilling dépaysement.
etymology: French, from 'dé-' (un-) + 'pays' (country); the feeling of being 'un-countried', out of one's element.

definition: The fluttering tangle of nerves and excitement just before a journey begins.
exampleSentence: The night before the flight she lay awake, heart drumming with resfeber.
etymology: Swedish, from 'resa' (journey) + 'feber' (fever); the 'travel-fever' of anticipation and anxiety combined.

definition: A truth that everyone knows but, by silent agreement, no one says aloud.
exampleSentence: His drinking was the family mokita, circled around at every dinner but never named.
etymology: Kilivila, of the Trobriand Islands of Papua New Guinea; the truth all agree to leave unspoken.

definition: A frenzy of yearning for something impossible to attain.
exampleSentence: His nympholepsy for a vanished, idealized past kept him from ever living in the present.
etymology: From Greek 'nympholēptos', 'seized by nymphs'; the ancients believed such ecstasy struck those who glimpsed a nymph. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A gullible person who will credulously swallow whatever they are told.
exampleSentence: Every conspiracy thread found a fresh gobemouche ready to believe and repost it.
etymology: French, from 'gober' (to gulp down) + 'mouche' (fly); literally a 'fly-swallower', mouth hanging open. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep-rooted sense of honour, dignity and duty toward family and community.
exampleSentence: Out of filotimo the old fisherman refused payment for ferrying the stranded family home.
etymology: Greek φιλότιμο, from 'philos' (love) + 'timi' (honour); literally 'love of honour', a cardinal Greek virtue.

definition: Stoic inner grit that keeps you going long after reason says to quit.
exampleSentence: It took pure sisu to finish the marathon on a sprained ankle in the sleet.
etymology: Finnish, from 'sisus' (the insides, the gut); a near-mythic Finnish ideal of resolve in adversity.

definition: The intuitive art of reading a room and sensing others' unspoken moods.
exampleSentence: She had the nunchi to change the subject the instant the table went quiet.
etymology: Korean 눈치, from 'nun' (eye); literally 'eye-measure', the quick gauging of a situation through subtle cues.

definition: The gentle, bittersweet sadness felt at the fleetingness of all beautiful things.
exampleSentence: Watching the petals scatter, she was filled with mono no aware for the brief spring.
etymology: Japanese 物の哀れ, from 'mono' (things) + 'aware' (pathos); the term was central to the eighteenth-century scholar Motoori Norinaga's literary criticism.

definition: The genuine happiness and satisfaction a person draws from their own work.
exampleSentence: The bakery hummed with an arbejdsglæde you could taste in every loaf.
etymology: Danish, from 'arbejde' (work) + 'glæde' (joy); literally 'work-joy'. Listed in Den Danske Ordbog.

definition: A cosy, low-key Friday night spent unwinding at home with snacks and loved ones.
exampleSentence: Blankets, tacos and a film: their fredagsmys was sacred after a long week.
etymology: Swedish, from 'fredag' (Friday) + 'mys' (cosiness); first appearing in Swedish print in 1994 and entering the SAOL dictionary in 2006.

definition: The giddy, fluttering thrill of a romantic or exciting moment.
exampleSentence: Just remembering his text gave her a fresh wave of kilig.
etymology: Tagalog; added to the Oxford English Dictionary in March 2016, its earliest cited use being 1981 in the Diliman Review.

definition: Beautifully understated and austere, with an elegance that deepens with age.
exampleSentence: The worn leather satchel had a shibui charm no new bag could match.
etymology: Japanese 渋い, originally 'astringent' (as of an unripe persimmon); transferred to a quiet, restrained, time-deepened beauty.

definition: Looking attractive only from a distance, the appeal evaporating up close.
exampleSentence: From across the bar he seemed striking, but it turned out he was purely layogenic.
etymology: Philippine English, from Tagalog 'layo' (distance) + the suffix '-genic' (as in photogenic); good-looking at a remove.

definition: Unusually and constantly sensitive to the cold.
exampleSentence: So friolero was she that she wore wool socks indoors through June.
etymology: Spanish, from 'frío' (cold) + the suffix '-ero'; describing a person who feels the cold acutely. Recorded by the Real Academia Española.

definition: Giving confident opinions on matters well beyond one's actual knowledge.
exampleSentence: His ultracrepidarian lectures on medicine annoyed every doctor at the dinner.
etymology: From Latin 'ne ultra crepidam' ('not beyond the sandal'), the painter Apelles' rebuke to a meddling cobbler in Pliny; coined as an English word by William Hazlitt around 1819.

definition: Effortlessly chic and refined, with a worldly stylishness that never tries too hard.
exampleSentence: Her plain grey coat and single pin were unmistakably iki.
etymology: Japanese 粋; the Edo-period merchant-class aesthetic analysed in Kuki Shūzō's 1930 treatise 'The Structure of Iki' as a blend of coquetry, composure and resignation.

definition: Floating in the giddy euphoria of beginning to fall in love.
exampleSentence: He grinned at his phone all morning, hopelessly forelsket.
etymology: Norwegian and Danish, the past participle of 'forelske seg' (to fall in love); the intoxicating first rush of new love.

definition: Boldly self-confident, cheeky and a little flashily daring.
exampleSentence: The wee one strode onstage gallus as you like and belted the first note.
etymology: Scots, possibly from 'gallows' (one fit for the gallows, hence reckless); now an admiring word for swagger. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Habitually gloomy, taciturn and darkly sardonic in temperament.
exampleSentence: He gave a saturnine half-smile and went back to brooding over his coffee.
etymology: From Latin 'Saturnus'; in medieval astrology, those born under the slow, cold planet Saturn were thought to be sluggish and grave.

definition: Warmly friendly, kindly and snugly comfortable, of a person or place.
exampleSentence: The wee couthie pub welcomed us in from the rain with a roaring fire.
etymology: Scots, from 'couth' (known, familiar, kindly); the opposite of the now-common 'uncouth'. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Elegantly harmonious, with every part fitting neatly and gracefully together.
exampleSentence: The essay's concinnous structure made each argument slide effortlessly into the next.
etymology: From Latin 'concinnus' (skilfully put together, neat); harmony achieved through fine proportion.

definition: Given to wandering about at night.
exampleSentence: His noctivagant habits meant the city's empty 3 a.m. streets felt like home.
etymology: From Latin 'nox, noctis' (night) + 'vagari' (to wander); a night-wanderer.

definition: Spontaneously playful, done for the sheer fun of it.
exampleSentence: Her ludic doodles crept into the margins of every serious report.
etymology: From French 'ludique', from Latin 'ludus' (play, game); pertaining to undirected, joyful play.

definition: Just the right amount — neither too much nor too little.
exampleSentence: He poured a lagom measure of coffee: enough to wake up, not enough to jitter.
etymology: Swedish, from an archaic dative plural of 'lag' (law), meaning 'according to custom'; the popular 'laget om' Viking mead-horn origin is a debunked folk etymology.

definition: Mysteriously entrancing, as if possessing a hidden, oracular power.
exampleSentence: The cellist drew an orphic hush over the entire candlelit hall.
etymology: From Orpheus, the Greek musician whose song could charm beasts, stones and even the dead; hence mystically beautiful and spellbinding.

definition: Worn out, exhausted and feeling a bit under the weather.
exampleSentence: After the night shift she felt fair wabbit and crawled straight into bed.
etymology: Scots; an expressive word for being drained or run-down. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: To shed every inhibition and let yourself go in the thick of enjoyment.
exampleSentence: By midnight even the shy accountant had begun to desbundar on the dance floor.
etymology: Brazilian Portuguese; to cast off restraint and surrender fully to fun.

definition: To keep eating a delicious meal well past fullness simply because it tastes so good.
exampleSentence: I meant to save half, but the khinkali were so good I shemomechama'd the lot.
etymology: Georgian შემომეჭამა; roughly 'I accidentally ate the whole thing', a passive admission that the food won.

definition: To shift scaldingly hot food around in your open mouth to keep it from burning you.
exampleSentence: He bit the molten pizza too soon and had to pelinti, eyes watering.
etymology: Buli, of Ghana; literally 'to move hot food around in the mouth' rather than spit it out.

definition: To sicken or weary someone with an excess of sweetness, whether of food or sentiment.
exampleSentence: The dessert was lovely at first but its syrup soon began to empalagar.
etymology: Spanish; to cloy or sate to the point of distaste. Recorded by the Real Academia Española.

definition: To do nothing on purpose, idling without aim or guilt.
exampleSentence: On Sundays she simply niksens by the window, watching the street go by.
etymology: Dutch, from 'niks' (nothing); the deliberate, restorative practice of doing nothing at all.

definition: To scratch your head in the hope of jogging loose a forgotten memory.
exampleSentence: He stood in the doorway to pana po'o, trying to recall why he'd come in.
etymology: Hawaiian; literally to scratch the head ('po'o') to help retrieve something forgotten.

definition: To be stirred to tears by something deeply touching.
exampleSentence: The old film never fails to commuovere her, right at the final goodbye.
etymology: Italian, from Latin 'commovere' (to stir up, agitate); to be moved warmly and tearfully within.

definition: To walk on tiptoe across sand or ground too hot to bear underfoot.
exampleSentence: We had to hanyauku the last stretch of beach to reach the cool of the water.
etymology: Rukwangali, of Namibia; recorded in the 1994 Bukenkango Rukwangali–English dictionary (Kloppers & Bredell).

definition: In strict confidence; secretly and off the record.
exampleSentence: The deal was negotiated sub rosa, months before any public announcement.
etymology: Latin, literally 'under the rose'; a rose hung above a meeting once signalled that all said beneath it was secret.

definition: Out in the open air at night, sleeping under the bare sky and stars.
exampleSentence: We abandoned the stuffy tent and slept à la belle étoile by the embers.
etymology: French, literally 'under the beautiful star'; spending the night outdoors with no roof but the heavens.

definition: In a secretive, muddled and disorderly fashion.
exampleSentence: The plans were drawn up hugger-mugger, and no two people agreed on them.
etymology: English, of uncertain sixteenth-century origin; long used by Shakespeare and others for furtive, confused concealment.

definition: At full gallop; headlong and at great speed.
exampleSentence: The children went tantivy down the hill the moment the gate swung open.
etymology: English, seventeenth-century, perhaps imitative of a galloping horse's hoofbeats; also a hunting cry.
